claims.text: Ligand complexation equalizes the reduction potentials of the noble-metal precursors.
Rapid thermal-shock heating causes the complexed Au, Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh precursors to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Nearly simultaneous precursor reduction produces uniform nucleation.
Uniform nucleation produces homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Without reduction-potential control, the metal precursors reduce sequentially.
Sequential reduction causes phase separation.
Sequential reduction causes uncontrolled particle morphologies.
The proposed material comprises Au, Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh precursors deposited on a high-surface-area carbon support.
Millisecond-scale heating above 500°C can enforce simultaneous reduction of the five precursors.
The degree of homogeneous nucleation determines the degree of uniform atomic mixing.
Metals that nucleate at different times undergo sequential nucleation.
Different nucleation times result in elemental or phase segregation.
Ligand complexation followed by rapid thermal shock will yield more homogeneous alloying than the baseline lacking complexation.
The intervention will maximize surface-atom exposure.
The intervention will reduce the decomposition or sintering temperature.
The baseline will exhibit phase separation and elemental segregation.
The baseline will exhibit non-uniform morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles on high-surface-area carbon under rapid thermal-shock conditions.
The mechanism may not apply when ligand complexation cannot adequately equalize precursor reduction potentials or when kinetics, thermodynamics, or synthesis environments differ fundamentally.
Residual differences in reduction potentials may cause partial phase segregation.

contradictions.description: The intervention, baseline, and falsification design compare ligand-complexed and uncomplexed samples that both receive rapid thermal shock, whereas the conditions field describes rapid thermal shock versus a moderate incremental-heating protocol. Thus, it is unclear whether complexation, heating protocol, or both are intended to differ between the controlled groups.
